chapters.title: Locating Places on the Earth
chapters.summary: How maps work, and how latitude, longitude and time let us find any place on Earth.

lessons.title: Maps: your treasure guide

activities.prompt: Ready to explore what a tiny treasure guide might show you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Map Treasure
activities.body:
Imagine you hold a treasure guide. A map shows where things are and how to get to them. You look at the surface from above. An atlas is a collection of maps.

First, you visit physical maps. They mainly show natural features, such as mountains, oceans and rivers. Political maps show countries or states, boundaries and cities. Thematic maps show one specific kind of information.

Your guide uses distance, direction and symbols. The map's scale lets a huge place fit on small paper. On the small-city map, 1 cm equals 500 m. On the India map, 2.5 cm in print stands for 500 km on the ground.

You next learn the four main directions: north, east, south and west. These are called cardinal directions. Other directions include northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest. Most maps have an arrow marked N, pointing north.

Finally, you unpack the map's symbols. These represent buildings, roads and natural features. Symbols help because there is not enough space to draw everything. The Survey of India has fixed a set of symbols for maps of India.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A map is a treasure guide
activities.body:
A **map** shows you where things are. It shows how to get there. It is like a treasure guide!

A map is a **drawing** of a place. You see the place from the **top**.
keyPoints: A map is a drawing of a place seen from the top.
An **atlas** is a book of maps.
activities.explanation: Next time you see a map, ask yourself: which way is the top?

activities.prompt: What is an atlas?
options: One big map on a wall
activities.explanation: An atlas is a book with many maps. Think of it as a library of maps.

activities.prompt: A map shows a place as seen from the side.
activities.explanation: A map shows a place from the top.

activities.title: Three kinds of maps
activities.body:
There are different kinds of maps.

**Physical maps** show natural things, like mountains, oceans and rivers.

**Political maps** show countries, states, boundaries and cities.

**Thematic maps** show one kind of information.
keyPoints: Physical: mountains, oceans, rivers.
Political: countries, states, boundaries, cities.
Thematic: one kind of information.
activities.explanation: Remember: physical maps show natural things. Political maps show countries, states, boundaries and cities.

activities.prompt: Match each map word to its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each kind of map has its own job. Read each one slowly. Then the match is clear.

activities.prompt: You want a map. It shows all the States of India and their capitals. Which kind of map is it?
activities.explanation: A map of India with its States and capitals is a political map.

activities.prompt: Which of these does a physical map mainly show?
options: Only one special kind of information
activities.explanation: A physical map shows natural things. Examples are mountains, oceans and rivers.

activities.title: The three parts of a map
activities.body:
Every map has three important parts: **distance**, **direction** and **symbols**.

In the next lesson, you will meet each one.
keyPoints: Distance
Direction
Symbols
activities.explanation: Distance, direction and symbols: you will meet all three next.

activities.prompt: A map has three important parts: distance, direction and ______.
activities.hint: They are small signs that show real things, like a school or a river.
activities.explanation: Symbols, direction and distance are the three important parts of a map.

lessons.title: Distance, direction and symbols

activities.prompt: How can we find any place on Earth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Trip Around Coordinates
activities.body:
Imagine holding a globe and wondering how a flat map shows our round Earth. You notice that the Earth is nearly a sphere, slightly flattened at the poles.

Next, you try to peel an orange and flatten its skin. The peel tears, because a sphere cannot be shown accurately on flat paper. A globe is a sphere with a map drawn on it. So, it represents the Earth better than a flat map.

Now, you watch a pawn move from d2 to d4 on a chessboard. A letter and a number name each square. Together, these two coordinates identify the square precisely.

After that, you enter a market and count its rows of shops. Your friend points to the 7th shop in the 5th row. Two numbers give that shop a precise place. Both places are located through their two coordinates. A similar system of coordinates is used in maps. It helps you find the location of any place.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Scale: a big place on small paper
activities.body:
How can a huge place fit on a small piece of paper? The map's **scale** does it!

Suppose the scale is **1 cm = 500 m**. Then every 1 cm on the map stands for 500 m on the ground.
keyPoints: The scale lets a huge place fit on small paper.
1 cm = 500 m means 1 cm on paper is 500 m on the ground.
activities.explanation: Scale is how a giant place fits on a tiny page.

activities.title: Use a map scale

tasks.then: Multiply by the scale to get the real distance.

tasks.say: At 25 km per cm, measure 8 cm.

activities.takeaway: A scale turns distance on a map into distance on the ground.
activities.explanation: A scale turns distance on a map into distance on the ground.

activities.prompt: What lets a huge place fit on a small piece of paper?
activities.explanation: The scale helps. Each centimetre on the map means a real distance on the ground.

activities.prompt: The scale is 1 cm = 500 m. So 1 cm on the map is ______ m on the ground.
activities.hint: Read the scale again: 1 cm means 500 m.
activities.explanation: On this map, 1 cm means 500 m on the ground.

activities.prompt: On a map, 1 cm stands for 500 m. Two places are 2 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
activities.explanation: 1 cm is 500 m. So 2 cm is 500 m + 500 m = 1,000 m.
derived: 250 m and 2,000 m are wrong options

activities.title: Directions
activities.body:
On the small-city map, **north** is at the top. Moving clockwise, the next directions are **east**, **south** and **west**. These four are the **cardinal directions**.

In between are northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest.

Most maps have an arrow marked **N**. It points north.
keyPoints: North, east, south, west: the cardinal directions.
NE, SE, SW, NW are in between.
The arrow marked N points north.
activities.explanation: Tip: look for the arrow marked N. It always points north.

activities.prompt: Start at north. Go clockwise (the way clock hands move). Put the cardinal directions in order.
activities.explanation: From north, going clockwise, you reach east. Then south. Then west.

activities.prompt: Match each in-between direction with the two cardinal directions it lies between.
activities.explanation: The name tells you the answer: northeast combines north and east.

activities.title: Symbols: a map's secret code
activities.body:
A big map has no room for every school, river or temple. So map makers use **symbols**. A symbol is a small sign for a real thing.

The **Survey of India** has made standard symbols for maps of India.
keyPoints: A symbol is a small sign for a real thing.
The Survey of India made the symbols for maps of India.
activities.explanation: Well done for reading carefully.

activities.prompt: Why do maps use symbols?
options: No space to draw every building and river
A map has no names on it
activities.explanation: A map of a big city or country has no space to draw everything. A symbol shows each thing instead.

lessons.title: The round Earth and coordinates

activities.prompt: How do imaginary lines help us understand distance and climate?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Latitude
activities.body:
Imagine your journey on a rotating globe, starting at the top and looking down. You meet the North Pole, then travel to the South Pole. They are the fixed points at the globe’s top and bottom.

Your next stop is the Equator, halfway between the two poles. It is the largest circle on the globe. Its latitude is 0 degrees.

Latitude measures your distance from the Equator. Imagine an imaginary line running east-west, parallel to the Equator. This is a parallel of latitude.

As you move away from the Equator, the parallels become smaller. They shrink towards the poles. At the far ends, the poles lie at 90 degrees North and 90 degrees South.

Your journey also reveals changing climates. Near the Equator, the climate is generally hot. Moving away, it becomes more moderate, or temperate. Near the poles, it is colder, or frigid.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Why do we need a globe?
activities.body:
The Earth is nearly a **sphere**. A sphere is a round shape, like a ball. It is a little flat at the poles. The poles are the top and bottom.

A sphere cannot be drawn well on flat paper. Peel an orange. Try to make the peel flat. It tears!

A **globe** is a sphere with a map on it. So it shows the Earth better than a flat map.
keyPoints: The Earth is nearly a sphere.
A sphere tears when you try to make it flat.
A globe is a sphere with a map on it.
activities.explanation: The Earth is round. So a globe is the best shape for a map.

activities.title: Find places on the grid

tasks.then: South of the Equator, latitude is marked S.

activities.takeaway: Latitude says how far north or south a place is.
activities.explanation: Latitude says how far north or south a place is.

activities.prompt: The Earth is nearly a sphere.
activities.explanation: Yes! It is nearly a ball, a little flat at the poles (the top and bottom).

activities.prompt: What does the orange peel trick show?
options: A round shape cannot be made flat without tearing
Oranges are bigger than the Earth
activities.explanation: You cannot make the peel flat without tearing it. A sphere is a round ball shape. A sphere cannot be shown exactly on flat paper.

activities.prompt: A globe is a sphere. A ______ is drawn on it.
activities.hint: It helps you find places.
activities.explanation: A globe is a sphere. A map is drawn on it.

activities.prompt: Why does a globe show the Earth better than a flat map?
options: The globe and the Earth have the same shape
A flat map is never useful
activities.explanation: A globe and the Earth are both round. So a globe is a better picture of the Earth.

activities.title: Coordinates: two clues, one place
activities.body:
Think of a chessboard. Each square has a letter and a number. A pawn moves from **d2** to **d4**. This tells you exactly where it goes.

Or think of a market: “the 7th shop in the 5th row”.

Two clues together give one exact place. They are called **coordinates**. Maps use the same idea!
keyPoints: Two clues together give one exact place.
These clues are called coordinates.
Maps use coordinates to find any place.
activities.explanation: Two clues, one place. You will use this idea again and again.

activities.prompt: A friend says, “Meet me at the 7th shop in the 5th row.” What do the two numbers do?
options: Together they show one exact place
They show the price of the shop
They show how big the market is
activities.explanation: A row number and a shop number together tell your friend the exact place.

activities.prompt: In chess, d2 and d4 are examples of ______.
activities.hint: The word starts with the letter c.
activities.explanation: A letter and a number, like d2 or d4, are coordinates. They name one square exactly.

activities.prompt: One number is enough to find a place exactly on a map.
activities.explanation: You need two numbers. These are called coordinates. A map uses a pair of numbers, like a chess square.

lessons.title: Latitude: lines around the Earth

activities.prompt: How can we describe a place on Earth using lines?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Along Longitude
activities.body:
Imagine you are setting out across Earth. You want to describe exactly where you are. Each meridian is a half-circle that runs from one pole to the other.

To measure longitude, you first need a reference point: the Prime Meridian. In 1884, some nations chose the meridian through Greenwich as the international Prime Meridian. Greenwich is in London, England, and this meridian is 0 degrees longitude.

Your longitude tells you your distance from the Prime Meridian, travelling along the Equator. It increases from 0 to 180 degrees, east or west. You can show its direction with E or W.

Round figures include these examples. New York is 74 degrees W, while Delhi is 77 degrees E. Tokyo lies at 140 degrees E.

Latitude and longitude work together as the two coordinates of a place. For example, Delhi lies at about 29 degrees N and 77 degrees E. Together, latitudes and longitudes form a grid called grid lines. The Equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The Prime Meridian divides Earth into the Western and Eastern Hemispheres.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: The poles and the Equator
activities.body:
Spin a globe. Two points at the top and bottom stay still. They are the **North Pole** and the **South Pole**.

Halfway between them, a line runs around the middle of the Earth. It is the **Equator**.
keyPoints: The two poles are the fixed points at the top and bottom.
The Equator is halfway between them.
activities.explanation: Picture the Equator as a belt around the Earth\u2019s middle.

activities.title: Find places on the grid

tasks.then: South of the Equator, latitude is marked S.

activities.takeaway: Latitude says how far north or south a place is.
activities.explanation: Latitude says how far north or south a place is.

activities.prompt: What is halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole?
activities.explanation: The Equator is halfway between the two poles.

activities.prompt: On a spinning globe, the two poles do not move. They are at the top and bottom.
activities.explanation: Yes! The poles stay still while the rest of the globe turns.

activities.title: Latitude
activities.body:
**Latitude** tells you how far a place is from the Equator.

Stand on the Equator. Then walk towards a pole. At any point, draw an imaginary line (not a real line) from east to west. It is parallel to the Equator. It is a **parallel of latitude**. It makes a circle around the Earth.
keyPoints: Latitude is how far a place is from the Equator.
A parallel of latitude runs east to west.
activities.explanation: Latitude is about north and south of the Equator.

activities.prompt: What does latitude measure?
options: How far a place is from the Equator
activities.explanation: Latitude measures the distance from the Equator.

activities.prompt: Which way does a parallel of latitude run?
options: East to west, parallel to the Equator
activities.explanation: Parallels run east to west. They are parallel to the Equator.

activities.title: Degrees
activities.body:
Latitude is measured in **degrees**.

The Equator is **0°**. The poles are **90° North** and **90° South**.

The Equator is the largest circle. The circles get smaller as you go towards the poles.
keyPoints: Equator: 0°.
North Pole: 90°N. South Pole: 90°S.
Circles get smaller towards the poles.
activities.explanation: Look for the little circle: 30\u00b0 means thirty degrees.

activities.prompt: Match each place with its latitude.
activities.explanation: The Equator is 0°. Each pole is 90° away from it, 90°N and 90°S.

activities.title: Latitude and climate
activities.body:
Latitude and **climate** are connected.

Around the Equator, the climate is generally **hot**. As you travel towards a pole, it becomes more **moderate**, or mild. Closer to the poles, it grows **colder**.
keyPoints: Near the Equator: hot.
In between: mild.
Near the poles: cold.
activities.explanation: Hot near the Equator, cold near the poles, mild in between.

activities.prompt: You go from the Equator to the North Pole. Put the climate in order.
activities.explanation: The climate is hot at the Equator. It is mild in the middle. Near the pole, it is cold.

lessons.title: Longitude: lines from pole to pole

activities.prompt: Why did India once have its own prime meridian?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: India's Own Middle Line
activities.body:
Imagine setting out on a journey through India's past. You find that India's prime meridian came many centuries before Europe's.

But this line had a special name, madhya rekha, meaning “middle line”. You follow it to Ujjayini, known today as Ujjain. This city was a reputed centre for astronomy.

Here, you meet the work of Indian astronomers. They knew about latitude and longitude. They also understood the need for a zero, or prime, meridian. Varahamihira, a famous astronomer, lived and worked here about 1,500 years ago.

You now wonder why some ancient cities sit a little away from the line. Measuring longitude required accurate timekeeping, which was not as precise then. This difficulty explains why some ancient cities lay a little away from it.

Your tour also shows India's great north-south and east-west reach. Its latitudes extend approximately from 8 degrees N to 37 degrees N. Its longitudes extend approximately from 68 degrees E to 97 degrees E. You can picture this wide country stretching across many lines of latitude and longitude.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meridians of longitude
activities.body:
Imagine the shortest line from the North Pole to the South Pole. This line is a **meridian of longitude**.

Meridians are half-circles. Each one goes from one pole to the other.
keyPoints: A meridian runs from pole to pole.
It is a half-circle.
activities.explanation: Parallels go east to west. Meridians go from pole to pole.

activities.title: Cross the Prime Meridian

tasks.then: West of Greenwich, longitude is marked W.

activities.takeaway: Longitude says how far east or west a place is.
activities.explanation: Longitude says how far east or west a place is.

activities.prompt: Which line runs from one pole to the other?
activities.explanation: Meridians of longitude are half-circles. They go from one pole to the other. Parallels of latitude run east to west.

activities.title: The Prime Meridian
activities.body:
To measure longitude, we need a starting line. It is called the **Prime Meridian**.

In **1884**, some countries agreed to use the meridian through **Greenwich**. Greenwich is in London, England. This line is marked **0°** longitude.
keyPoints: The Prime Meridian is the starting line for longitude.
It passes through Greenwich, in London.
It is 0°.
activities.explanation: Counting longitude starts at Greenwich, in London.

activities.prompt: The starting line for longitude is called the ______ Meridian.
activities.hint: It is the line marked 0° longitude.
activities.explanation: The Prime Meridian is the starting line for measuring longitude.

activities.prompt: The Prime Meridian goes through a place in London. What is its name?
activities.explanation: The Prime Meridian goes through Greenwich, an area of London in England.

activities.title: East and west
activities.body:
**Longitude** tells how far a place is from the Prime Meridian. You measure it east or west along the Equator.

It goes from **0°** to **180°**. We add **E** for east. We add **W** for west. (180° has no letter.)

Delhi is 77°E. Tokyo is 140°E. New York is 74°W.
keyPoints: Longitude: how far from the Prime Meridian.
0° to 180°, with E or W.
activities.explanation: E means east of the Prime Meridian. W means west of it.

activities.prompt: Delhi is at 77°E. What does E mean?
options: Delhi is east of the Prime Meridian
Delhi is at the North Pole
activities.explanation: E means east. Delhi is 77° east of the Prime Meridian.

activities.prompt: Match each city with its longitude.
activities.explanation: Delhi and Tokyo are east of the Prime Meridian. New York is west of it.

activities.title: Latitude and longitude together
activities.body:
Latitude and longitude are the two **coordinates** of a place. Together, they can find any place on Earth!

“Delhi lies at about **29°N** latitude and **77°E** longitude.”

All these lines make a **grid**.

The Equator divides Earth into the **Northern** and **Southern** Hemispheres. The Prime Meridian divides it into the **Western** and **Eastern** Hemispheres.
keyPoints: Latitude + longitude = coordinates.
The Equator: Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
The Prime Meridian: Western and Eastern Hemispheres.
activities.explanation: Latitude and longitude are the two coordinates we use to find a place.

activities.prompt: Delhi is at 29°N and 77°E. Which number is the latitude?
activities.explanation: Latitude is north or south of the Equator. 29°N is the latitude. 77°E is the longitude.

activities.prompt: The Equator splits the Earth into Eastern and Western Hemispheres (halves of the Earth).
activities.explanation: The Equator makes the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The Prime Meridian makes the Western and Eastern ones.

lessons.title: India’s own middle line

activities.prompt: Why might clocks look different as you travel around the world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Time
activities.body:
Imagine standing on the Earth while it turns beneath you.
It spins from west to east, making a full turn every 24 hours.
A full turn covers 360 degrees, or 15 degrees each hour.

Now, begin at Greenwich with the clock showing noon.
Moving east, you add one hour for every 15 degrees.
At 15 degrees east, it is 1 pm; at 30 degrees east, 2 pm.
Moving west reverses the pattern.
At 15 degrees west, it is 11 am; at 30 degrees west, 10 am.

Next, you visit Porbandar and Tinsukia in India.
They are about 30 degrees of longitude apart.
Most countries use one standard time, based on a meridian passing through them.
India uses Indian Standard Time.
It runs 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time.

Farther on, you reach the International Date Line near 180 degrees longitude.
It lies opposite the Prime Meridian.
Crossing eastward, you subtract a day.
Crossing westward, you add one day, moving from Sunday to Monday.
The line bends in places to avoid dividing some countries into two days.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: India had a prime meridian too
activities.body:
Many centuries before Europe, **India** had a prime meridian of its own!

It was called **madhya rekhā**, or “middle line”.

It passed through the city of **Ujjayinī**, which is Ujjain today. Ujjayinī was a famous centre for **astronomy**.
keyPoints: Many centuries before Europe, India had its own prime meridian.
It was called madhya rekhā, the middle line.
It passed through Ujjayinī (Ujjain).
activities.explanation: Long ago, Indian astronomers already used the idea of a zero line for longitude.

activities.prompt: Which city did India’s own prime meridian go through?
activities.explanation: India’s own prime meridian (madhya rekhā) went through Ujjayinī. Today it is Ujjain.

activities.prompt: India’s prime meridian was called madhya rekhā. It means “______ line”.
activities.hint: The answer is a short word. It means “in the centre”.
activities.explanation: Madhya rekhā means “middle line”.

activities.title: The astronomers of Ujjayinī
activities.body:
**Varahamihira** was a famous **astronomer**. An astronomer studies stars and planets. He lived and worked in Ujjayinī about **1,500 years ago**.

Indian astronomers knew about **latitude** and **longitude**. They knew they needed a prime meridian, the zero line.
keyPoints: Varahamihira worked in Ujjayinī about 1,500 years ago.
Indian astronomers knew about latitude and longitude.
activities.explanation: Well done for reading carefully.

activities.prompt: Indian astronomers did not know about latitude and longitude.
activities.explanation: Indian astronomers did know about latitude and longitude. They knew a prime meridian was needed.

activities.prompt: About how long ago did Varahamihira live in Ujjayinī?
activities.explanation: The book says Varahamihira lived and worked there about 1,500 years ago.

activities.title: Where is India on the globe?
activities.body:
India’s **latitudes** go from about **8°N to 37°N**.

Its **longitudes** go from about **68°E to 97°E**.
keyPoints: Latitudes: about 8°N to 37°N.
Longitudes: about 68°E to 97°E.
activities.explanation: These are rounded numbers, so we say \u201cabout\u201d.

activities.prompt: India’s latitudes go from about 8°N to ______°N.
activities.hint: It is a number in the thirties.
activities.explanation: India’s latitudes go from about 8°N to 37°N.

activities.prompt: Some old cities were a little away from the Ujjayinī meridian. Why?
options: People could not measure time well then. Finding longitude needs good time.
Those cities were in the sea.
activities.explanation: Finding longitude needs good timekeeping. Long ago, people could not measure time as well as they do today.

lessons.title: Time on a spinning Earth

activities.title: A spinning Earth
activities.body:
The Earth spins from **west to east**. One full turn takes **24 hours**.

A full turn is **360°**. So the Earth turns **15° every hour**, because 15 × 24 = 360.
keyPoints: One full turn takes 24 hours.
A full turn is 360°.
The Earth turns 15° every hour.
activities.explanation: Remember: 360\u00b0 in 24 hours is 15\u00b0 every hour.

activities.title: Travel through the time zones

tasks.then: At noon in Greenwich it is 1 pm here.
It is 10 am here: going west, clocks are behind.

activities.takeaway: Each 15 degrees of longitude is one hour.
activities.explanation: Each 15 degrees of longitude is one hour.

activities.prompt: The Earth makes one full turn in 24 hours.
activities.explanation: Yes! One full turn takes 24 hours.

activities.prompt: The Earth turns ______ degrees every hour.
activities.hint: A full turn is 360°. A day has 24 hours.
activities.explanation: 15 × 24 = 360, so the Earth turns 15° every hour.

activities.title: Local time
activities.body:
Going **east**, every 15° adds **one hour**. If it is noon at Greenwich, it is 1 pm at 15°E. It is 2 pm at 30°E.

Going **west**, it is the opposite. It is 11 am at 15°W. It is 10 am at 30°W.
keyPoints: East: add one hour for every 15°.
West: take away one hour for every 15°.
activities.explanation: East adds time. West takes time away.

activities.prompt: It is 12 noon in Greenwich. What is the local time at 15°E?
activities.explanation: Going east adds one hour for every 15°. So noon becomes 1 pm.

activities.prompt: It is 12 noon in Greenwich. What is the local time at 30°W?
activities.explanation: Going west takes away one hour for every 15°. At 30°W, that is two hours less: 10 am.

activities.title: One time for a whole country
activities.body:
A country with many local times would be confusing. So most countries follow one **standard time**. It is based on a meridian that passes through the country.

India uses **Indian Standard Time (IST)**. IST is **5 hours 30 minutes ahead** of **Greenwich Mean Time (GMT)**.
keyPoints: Most countries use one standard time.
IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
activities.explanation: One standard time keeps a whole country on the same clock.

activities.prompt: Why do most countries use one standard time?
options: Many local times are hard to use
activities.explanation: Many local times are hard to use. So one standard time is used.

activities.prompt: It is late afternoon. In Tinsukia (Assam), the Sun has set. In Porbandar (Gujarat), the Sun has not set. Their longitudes differ by about 30°. How many hours ahead is Tinsukia?
activities.explanation: The Earth turns 15° every hour. 30° ÷ 15° = 2 hours. Tinsukia is east of Porbandar. So its local time is 2 hours ahead. That is why it can be dark in Assam but still light in Gujarat.
derived: 1 hour and 3 hours are wrong options

activities.prompt: It is 12 noon in London. What time is it in India?
activities.explanation: Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich time. Add 5 hours 30 minutes to noon. So it is 5:30 pm.

lessons.title: Time zones and the Date Line

activities.title: Time zones
activities.body:
Standard times are grouped into **time zones**. The lines between zones are **not perfectly straight**. They **tend to follow** country borders.

Some big countries need more than one time zone. The **USA has six** time zones. **Russia has 11**.
keyPoints: Time zone lines tend to follow country borders.
The USA has six time zones. Russia has 11.
activities.explanation: Some big countries need more than one time zone.

activities.title: Travel through the time zones

tasks.then: At noon in Greenwich it is 1 pm here.
It is 10 am here: going west, clocks are behind.

activities.takeaway: Each 15 degrees of longitude is one hour.
activities.explanation: Each 15 degrees of longitude is one hour.

activities.prompt: Why are the lines between time zones not fully straight?
activities.explanation: The lines must match each country's standard time. So they often follow country borders.

activities.explanation: Russia has 11 time zones, so you change your watch 10 times.

activities.title: The International Date Line
activities.body:
The **International Date Line** is opposite the **Prime Meridian**. It is at about **180°** longitude.

If you cross it going **east**, you **subtract** (take away) **a day**. For example, it changes from Monday to Sunday.

If you cross it going **west**, you **add a day** (one more day). For example, it changes from Sunday to Monday.
keyPoints: The Date Line is at about 180°.
East: subtract a day.
West: add a day.
activities.explanation: East subtracts a day. West adds a day.

activities.prompt: Where is the International Date Line?
activities.explanation: The International Date Line is at about 180° longitude. It is opposite the Prime Meridian.

activities.prompt: A ship crosses the International Date Line going west. Before this, it was Sunday. What is the new day?
activities.explanation: Going west across the Date Line, you add a day. Sunday becomes Monday.

activities.prompt: The International Date Line is a completely straight line along 180°.
activities.explanation: It bends in some places. This stops some countries from having two different days.

lessons.title: The blue planet

activities.prompt: What secrets can you discover while touring our planet from space?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Earth's Water
activities.body:
Imagine you rise above Earth and look down. Its surface appears mostly blue because water covers almost three-fourths of it. Early astronauts called it the blue planet.

The brown patches are land. Together, they cover a little over one-fourth of the globe. A large body of land is called a landmass. A large continuous expanse of land is a continent.

The largest water bodies on Earth are called oceans. Oceans and continents are spread unevenly between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Both help shape Earth's climate. Their effects reach every living thing.

Oceans also have smaller extensions called seas, bays and gulfs. Most of Earth's water lies in the oceans. Yet seawater is salty and unfit for most land animals, including you.

Only a very small share of Earth's water is freshwater. You can find it in glaciers, rivers, lakes, the atmosphere and underground. Water underground has a special name: groundwater.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Why Earth looks blue
activities.body: Earth looks mostly blue from space because water covers almost three-fourths of its surface. Early astronauts called Earth the blue planet. Oceans are the largest water bodies on Earth. A landmass is a large body of land. A continent is a large continuous expanse of land. Oceans and continents shape Earth's climate and affect all life.
keyPoints: Water covers almost three-fourths of Earth's surface.
Early astronauts called Earth the blue planet.
Oceans and continents shape Earth's climate and affect all life.
activities.explanation: These facts explain Earth's colour, major land and water features, and their importance.

lessons.title: The five oceans

activities.prompt: How do the oceans connect, and what makes each one special?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Ocean Tour
activities.body:
Imagine a voyage across the world's oceans. You meet five: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern. The map lines between them are only conventions. Seawater constantly flows across oceans, sustaining a rich diversity of marine life.

Now compare their sizes. The Pacific is largest, followed by the Atlantic. The Indian Ocean is third largest, and the Southern Ocean is fourth. The Arctic Ocean is smallest.

You sail into the Indian Ocean. Asia bounds it to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east. The Southern Ocean lies to its south.

Beside India, you explore two parts. The Arabian Sea lies west, and the Bay of Bengal lies east. Andaman and Nicobar sit in the Bay of Bengal. Lakshadweep sits in the Arabian Sea.

Before your voyage ends, you learn two useful words. Marine means related to oceans and seas. Flora means plant life, while fauna means animal life. Together, these words describe plant and animal life in oceans.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet the five oceans
activities.body:
There are five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern. They are connected. Lines on a map are agreed boundaries. Seawater flows between them. It supports rich sea life.

The Pacific is the largest. The Atlantic is next. The Indian Ocean is third largest. The Southern is fourth largest. The Arctic is the smallest.
keyPoints: The five oceans are Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern.
Map lines are agreed boundaries, but seawater flows between oceans.
The Pacific is the largest ocean. The Arctic is the smallest.

lessons.title: Rain, storms and tsunamis

activities.prompt: Clouds, storms and ocean waves can change where we live. How do they do that?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Clouds, Storms and Tsunamis
activities.body:
You see white shapes on Earth from space. These shapes are large masses of clouds. Clouds bring rain to the continents. India’s monsoon rains begin in the ocean.

You learn that without such rains, agriculture and all life would suffer. Oceans often give rise to storms such as cyclones. They can cause widespread damage to coastal regions.

You meet a tsunami, a huge, powerful wave. Usually, a strong earthquake or volcanic eruption causes one on the ocean floor. It can travel thousands of kilometres and submerge coastal areas. Tsunamis are rare, but very destructive.

You remember 26 December 2004, when an earthquake caused a tsunami. It struck India and thirteen other countries around the Indian Ocean. More than two lakh people lost their lives. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands were severely affected. The coasts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala were severely affected.

You learn that many countries, including India, contribute to the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System. It can often detect tsunamis before a tsunami hits a coast. India has the National Disaster Management Authority for disaster events.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Rain, storms and tsunamis
activities.body: From space, clouds look white. Clouds bring rain to the land. India's monsoon rains start over the ocean. Oceans make cyclones. Cyclones can damage places near the coast. Earthquakes or volcanoes cause tsunamis. Tsunamis start at the bottom of the ocean. Tsunamis are huge waves. They travel thousands of kilometres. They flood areas near the coast. We can often find tsunamis before they reach the coast. Disaster management helps when people lose life or homes.
keyPoints: Clouds bring rain to the land.
Cyclones can damage places near the coast.
Tsunamis are huge, powerful waves.

lessons.title: Seven continents (or four, or five, or six)

activities.prompt: How many continents might be hiding in our world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Many Continents?
activities.body:
Imagine you are setting out on a world tour. You open your atlas and wonder how many continents you will visit. The answer may surprise you, because continents can be counted in several ways.

On your map, you see Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. You can count seven continents this way. This list is the one most widely adopted and used.

As you explore, you find that the count can change. North America and South America are generally two continents. However, you can also see them as one landmass.

Europe and Asia are generally two continents, although they form a single landmass. Geologists often regard them as one continent called Eurasia. Africa and Eurasia are generally two continents too. Sometimes, people regard these as one.

Before you finish, look closely at any continent diagram. It shows relative sizes, not actual shapes. The Northern Hemisphere also has more land than the Southern Hemisphere. Perhaps your atlas gives you seven continents, while other maps give you fewer.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How many continents?
activities.body: People count the world’s continents in different ways. Some count four, while others count five, six or seven. North and South America may be joined. Europe and Asia share one landmass, a large connected piece of land. This landmass is often called Eurasia. Africa and Eurasia may also be counted together. The seven-continent list is most widely used. A hemisphere is half of Earth. Inhabited means having people living there.
keyPoints: Continents can be counted in several ways.
Some joined landmasses may count as one continent.
The seven-continent list is most widely used.
activities.explanation: Different counting methods explain why people give different numbers of continents.

lessons.title: Islands and the icy south

activities.prompt: What can islands and the icy south teach us about our planet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Islands and the Icy South
activities.body:
Imagine a journey across the planet, where you explore land surrounded by water. An island is a smaller piece of land, with water on every side. There are lakhs of islands of very different sizes.

You find that continents are also surrounded by water, but their size keeps them from being islands. Greenland is the world's largest island. India has more than 1,300 small islands.

Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal. Lakshadweep Islands lie in the Arabian Sea. Your island tour now stretches across two different seas.

Your journey continues to Antarctica, a continent with a very cold climate and harsh environment. It is mostly ice, the white expanse at the bottom of the Earth picture. Since 1981, the Indian Antarctica Programme has explored this icy place. Here, you meet India's first scientific base station, established in 1983 and called Dakshin Gangotri.

The settlement where Indian scientists live has a library and even a post office. Indian scientists research the evolution of climate and environment here. You finish your tour understanding how islands and the icy south differ.

activities.title: Islands, continents and icy Antarctica
activities.body: Islands are small pieces of land with water on every side. Continents have water around them too, but they are very large. Lakhs means very many. India has two main island groups. Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal. Lakshadweep Islands lie in the Arabian Sea. Antarctica is a cold, icy continent where Indian scientists do research.
keyPoints: Islands have water on all sides.
Continents are too large to be islands.
Indian scientists research climate and environment in Antarctica.
activities.explanation: Antarctica is a continent, while Greenland is the largest island.

lessons.title: Oceans and life

activities.prompt: What amazing things are under the waves? How does the sea affect your life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tour of Ocean Life
activities.body:
Imagine your journey begins beside the sea. You watch the waves and wonder where their water goes next.

Oceans send rain to the continents as part of Earth's water cycle. Without oceans, there would be no rainfall, and Earth would be a desert. You see oceans as part of our living planet.

More than half of the world's oxygen comes from the oceans' flora. That is why oceans are called the planet's lungs. You also see that oceans regulate climate and sustain life.

On your tour, you learn that people use oceans and seas to migrate and trade. They have also conducted military campaigns and caught fish for food. Coastal people share tales of gods, goddesses, monsters and sea treasures.

During your visit, you learn of a serious problem. Several million tonnes of plastic waste enter the oceans each year. These wastes choke marine life. Overfishing also reduces marine life. The United Nations has designated June 8 as World Oceans Day. Protecting oceans is everyone's responsibility for the planet and humanity.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Why oceans matter
activities.body: Oceans are vital to life on Earth. They send rain to continents as part of the Earth's water cycle. Without oceans, rainfall would disappear and Earth would become a desert. Ocean plants (flora) produce more than half the world's oxygen. This is why oceans are called the planet's lungs. They also regulate climate and sustain life.
keyPoints: Oceans send rain and help the Earth's water cycle.
Without oceans, Earth would be a desert.
Ocean plants make oxygen and help sustain life.
activities.explanation: Oceans help bring rain, make oxygen and sustain life.

activities.title: Rain for the continents
activities.prompt: What do oceans send to the continents?
activities.explanation: Oceans send rain to the continents. This is part of the Earth's water cycle.

activities.title: Life without oceans

activities.explanation: Without oceans, there would be no rain. Earth would become a desert.

Part of the Earth's water cycle
Oceans are called the planet's lungs
activities.explanation: These pairs show what oceans do, and the Indian Navy motto. Varuna is linked to oceans, the sky and water.

activities.title: The planet's lungs
activities.prompt: Why are oceans called the planet's lungs?
options: They send rain to the continents.
Their plants make more than half the world's oxygen.
activities.explanation: Ocean plants (flora) make more than half the world's oxygen. This is why oceans are called the planet's lungs.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: landforms: three main types; mountains: their shapes and world locations; mountain environment and life; plateaus: raised land with broad surfaces.

lessons.title: Landforms: Three Main Types

activities.prompt: What makes Earth’s land look so different from place to place?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Touring Three Main Landforms
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a journey across land that looks different in every region. You might see many changing shapes along the way. You learn that a landform is a physical feature on Earth’s surface. Landforms can take millions of years to form.

Your tour begins with mountains. They are much higher than the surrounding landscape. You can recognise them by a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit. Some mountains are covered with snow because of their height.

At very high altitudes, snow may never melt. This can leave a mountain permanently snowcapped.

Next, you reach a plateau, one of the three main types. A plain completes the trio. Together, these three landforms show how greatly land can vary.

Landforms can have different climates. They also support varied plants and animals. People have adapted to all three main types. You may notice that different numbers of people live on them around the world.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What are landforms?
activities.body: Land looks very different in different places. A landform is a natural shape on Earth's surface. Landforms take millions of years to form. The three main types are mountains, plateaus and plains. A plateau is high, flat land. Each type has its own climate (usual weather), plants and animals. People have learned to live in all three.
keyPoints: A landform is a natural shape on Earth's surface.
The three main types are mountains, plateaus and plains.
Each landform has its own climate, plants and animals.
activities.explanation: Landforms shape the land around us. They take a very long time to form.

activities.prompt: A landform is a physical feature on Earth's surface.
activities.explanation: This is the plain meaning of a landform.

activities.prompt: There are three main types of landforms: ______, plateaus and plains.

activities.explanation: Mountains can be recognised by a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit.

activities.explanation: The wide base comes first. Then the slopes. The narrow summit is at the top.

lessons.title: Mountains: Their Shapes and World Locations

activities.prompt: Ready to discover what makes mountains look so different from one another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Mountain Shapes
activities.body:
Imagine a mountain tour through the Himalayas, the Alps and the Andes. These mountain ranges show you that mountains often gather in lines. Some ranges stretch for thousands of kilometres.

Meet Mount Everest and Kanchenjunga, the two highest peaks of the Himalayan range. Visit Mount Aconcagua, the highest peak of the Andes. In the Alps, Mont Blanc stands highest. You reach south India, where Anamudi, also called Anai Peak, is the highest mountain.

Not every high mountain belongs to a range. Kilimanjaro stands alone as an isolated mountain. You now compare a lone mountain with peaks gathered in ranges. Your guide shows you how hills are lower, less steep and more rounded than mountains.

Your tour next reaches the Aravalli Range, where the hills are much older. Here, erosion has rounded the hills over time. The Himalayas offer a different picture because they are relatively young mountains.

Mountains do not always keep the same shape. Upliftment and erosion continue to affect some mountains today. By comparing ranges, lone peaks and rounded hills, you learn to read their shapes.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet Some Famous Mountains
activities.body: Hills are lower, less steep and more rounded than mountains. The Himalayas, Alps and Andes are mountain ranges. Mount Everest and Kanchenjunga are the highest Himalayan peaks. Mount Aconcagua is highest in the Andes, while Mont Blanc is highest in the Alps. Mount Kilimanjaro is isolated. The Himalayas are relatively young. The Aravalli hills are older and rounded by erosion. Upliftment and erosion continue today.
keyPoints: Hills are lower, less steep and more rounded than mountains.
Mountain ranges contain famous peaks.
Some mountains are young, while others are older and changing.
activities.explanation: Mountains can be grouped by their shapes, ages and locations.

activities.prompt: What can you discover while travelling through a mountain environment?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Mountain Life
activities.body:
You begin your journey among rugged mountain terrain, where steep slopes shape the land ahead. Soon, you enter montane forests, forests that often cover mountain slopes. Tall conifer trees rise around you, their thin, pointed leaves and cone-shaped forms reaching skyward.

Climb higher, and the trees gradually give way to grasses, mosses and lichen. This change in plant life feels like a new chapter on your journey. Nearby, mountain forests, rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves shelter diverse fauna.

Follow the Ganga, the largest river that originates in the Himalayas. Many tributaries join it, each bringing another river into the shared flow. Regular farming can be practised only in some mountain valleys. Terrace farming is done by cutting steps into mountain slopes.

Some communities prefer herding to agriculture in mountainous regions. Tourism often provides important income for some mountain communities. However, too many visitors can put pressure on the fragile mountain environment. Your tour ends among mountains with diverse fauna. You have passed forests, rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Life in the Mountains
activities.body: Mountain slopes often have montane forests. Conifers are tall, cone-shaped and have thin, pointed leaves. Higher up, trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen. Mountain forests, rivers, lakes, grasslands and caves have diverse fauna. Diverse fauna means many animals live there. Only some valleys allow regular farming. Terrace farming cuts steps into mountain slopes. Herding is often preferred to agriculture. Tourism often provides mountain communities with income.
keyPoints: Montane forests often cover mountain slopes.
Higher slopes have grasses, mosses and lichen.
Farming, herding and tourism shape mountain life.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how mountains shape forests, farming and daily life.

lessons.title: Plateaus: Raised Land with Broad Surfaces

activities.prompt: What can you discover while touring a plateau?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Plateaus
activities.body:
Imagine standing on a vast table of land. Its surface is more or less flat. You can look across its broad surface. You may wonder how such land formed.

During your journey, you meet plateaus of different ages. Some are young, while others are old in Earth’s history. You see heights from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres. Each view adds another chapter to your journey.

Now, you arrive at the Tibetan Plateau. It is the largest and highest plateau in the world. Its average altitude is 4,500 metres. Next, you visit the Deccan Plateau. It formed through volcanic activity millions of years ago.

Here, you look below your feet and notice the soil. Many plateaus have rocky soil. Lava plateaus often have rich black soil. Plateaus are rich in mineral deposits. Mining is therefore a major activity on plateaus. Finally, you hear rushing water. Many spectacular waterfalls are found on plateaus.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is a plateau?
activities.body:
A **plateau** is raised land. Its top is mostly flat. Its height can be a few hundred metres. It can also be several thousand metres.

Plateaus can be young or old. They have many mineral deposits. So mining is important.

Many have rocky soil. Lava plateaus often have rich black soil. Many waterfalls are found on them.
keyPoints: A plateau has a mostly flat surface.
Plateau heights are very different.
Plateaus can be young or old.
activities.explanation: Plateaus are high, flat lands with many important features.

activities.prompt: The top of a plateau is mostly flat.
activities.explanation: Yes. A plateau has a wide top that is mostly flat.

activities.prompt: Which plateau is the biggest and highest in the world?

activities.explanation: This sentence matches many plateaus with rocky soil. It matches lava plateaus with black soil.

lessons.title: Plains and River Life

activities.prompt: What makes river plains special for people, farms and communities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Plains and River Life
activities.body:
Imagine yourself walking across a vast plain. The land stretches far, with gentle rises and dips. Plains generally rise no more than 300 metres above sea level. As you travel, rivers slowly carry sediment and spread it across the land. Their deposits create very fertile soil.

From your journey, you learn why the first civilisations grew near rivers in fertile plains. You discover rich soil beside the water. You also learn that many people live on plains around the world.

Now you enter the Ganga plain. About 40 crore people live here. This is over one-fourth of India’s population. You see people fish in rivers and farm fertile land. These are important occupations in the plain.

You can travel easily by boat because plains rivers have a gentle slope. Irrigation helps farmers grow more food. However, it also reduces groundwater.

Later, you visit a sacred river location. Here, many communities hold festivals, ceremonies and rituals. As you return, you understand why plains and rivers support life together. You remember the flat land, fertile soil and easy river travel.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Life on the Plains
activities.body: Plains are big, flat lands. Some plains are gently rolling. They are usually no more than 300 metres above sea level. Rivers leave **sediments** (mud and soil) on them. This makes the soil **fertile**, good for growing crops. The first civilisations grew up near rivers on these plains. Many people live there. Farming, river fishing, easy river travel and holy festivals are important parts of river life.
keyPoints: Plains are flat or gently rolling.
Plains are usually no more than 300 metres above sea level.
River sediments make plains fertile.
activities.explanation: Plains have rich soil, calm rivers and lively communities.

activities.explanation: Correct! River sediments make the soil of plains very fertile.

activities.explanation: Correct! About 40 crore people live in the Ganga plain.

activities.title: Good Things and Problems
activities.body: Irrigation means bringing water to farms. It helps farms grow more food. But irrigation also lowers groundwater. Groundwater is water under the ground. River life includes farming and fishing. Rivers on plains are easy to travel on. The land slopes down gently. Many communities hold festivals and ceremonies at holy river places. These facts show how river plains help work, travel and community life.
keyPoints: Irrigation helps farms grow more food.
Irrigation also lowers groundwater.
Holy river places are used for community events.
activities.explanation: This shows the good and bad of irrigation.

activities.title: Deserts and the Bigger Picture
activities.body:
You begin your journey among deserts. You meet unique plants and animals in each one.

First, you visit the Sahara in Africa and the Thar in India. Both are hot deserts. Next, you travel to the Gobi Desert in Asia. Here, you find a cold desert.

As you continue, you meet people who live in most deserts. Despite harsh living conditions, humans have adapted to these places. You see how people can live in difficult surroundings.

Then, your guide opens a book of ancient Tamil Sangam poetry. It describes five landscapes called tiṇais. You notice that their classification differs from the three main types.

This wider view helps you understand the bigger picture. Landforms form an important part of culture around the world. Every landform offers both challenges and opportunities.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Deserts, Landforms and Culture
activities.body: Deserts have unique plants and animals. The Sahara and Thar are hot deserts. The Gobi is cold. Humans have adapted to most deserts despite harsh conditions. Ancient Tamil Sangam poetry describes five landscape types called tiṇais. A tiṇai is one type in this classification. They use a different landform classification from the three main types. Landforms matter to culture around the world. Every landform offers both challenges and opportunities.
keyPoints: Hot deserts include the Sahara and Thar.
The Gobi is a cold desert.
Five tiṇais use a different classification from the three main types.
activities.explanation: Deserts show how living things adapt and how landforms connect with culture.

chapters.title: Timeline and Sources of History
chapters.summary: In this chapter: how we learn about the past; how time is measured in history; timelines, centuries and millenniums; what are the sources of history?.

lessons.title: How We Learn About the Past

activities.prompt: What can we discover by looking back?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Learning Earth's Past
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a journey through the Earth's very, very long history. You find that humans occupy only a tiny and recent part of this story. The journey begins with people who study the history of the Earth.

First, you meet geologists. They study features of the Earth, such as soil, stones, hills, mountains and rivers. Some are trained to uncover secrets beneath the Earth's surface. You watch them examine these features to understand the past.

Next, you meet palaeontologists. They study fossils of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago. Some fossils show impressions of footprints. Others preserve parts of plants and animals.

Then, you meet archaeologists. They study the past by digging up remains left by people, plants and animals. You see them dig up these remains.

lessons.title: How Time Is Measured in History

activities.prompt: How do people count years before and after today?

activities.title: A Tour Through Time
activities.body:
Imagine you are a time traveller visiting different societies. Each society and culture has developed its own way of measuring time. So your journey begins with many calendars.

Important events, like a ruler's reign beginning, can mark a new era. One calendar uses the conventional year of Jesus Christ's birth as its starting point. You count years forward from that chosen point.

The Gregorian calendar has twelve months, adding up to 365 days. Among 1800, 1900 and 2000, only 2000 was a leap year. Careful checking helps you understand such differences.

You also meet Hindu, Muslim, Jewish and Chinese calendars, plus others. These calendars are also used across different societies and cultures. Each system measures time in its own cultural way.

After the starting point, the period is called the Common Era, or CE. Before it, the period is called Before Common Era, or BCE. The Gregorian calendar has no year zero. For a BCE date and a CE date, add them and subtract one. For example, 2 BCE to 2 CE spans three years.

activities.title: A Walk Through Time
activities.body:
Imagine you enter a room where history stretches along one long line. A timeline is a useful tool for marking historical events. It shows a sequence of dates and events within a period.

As you walk, notice how the line keeps events in order. This helps you understand the order in which historical events happened. Sometimes, a dotted part shows that a period has been skipped.

Now look at two markers on the line. The timeline shows that the Buddha was born before Jesus. A decade is a period of ten years. A century is any period of 100 years.

Next, you reach a new part of your journey. The 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100. A millennium is any period of 1,000 years. The 3rd millennium CE began in 2001 and will end in 3000.

Step back, and you see the whole tour. Timelines do more than place events. They help you understand the order in which historical events happened.

activities.title: Following History's Clues
activities.body:
Imagine you are beginning a journey into the past. Your guide is a source: a place, person, text or object. Each can give you information about what happened.

You visit a place and inspect its objects and structures. Every object or structure can tell a story about the past. At home, family histories can be learnt from photographs and diaries. Identity cards and family memories can add more clues.

You then follow clues through literature, a key group of historical sources. Archaeological and oral sources can also provide information about history. Historians work with archaeologists, epigraphists, anthropologists and other experts. Together, these sources help put historical events together.

You collect as many sources as you can find. Sometimes, different sources confirm the same information. Other times, they disagree, so you decide which source you trust more. You may still have missing pieces in your historical puzzle.

You can also study ancient climates and excavated materials. These studies give fresh insights into the past. Finally, you build a careful account from the strongest clues available.

activities.title: A Journey into Early Life
activities.body:
Imagine beginning your journey through human history. You will discover that modern humans have walked the Earth for about 300,000 years. Yet this journey is only a tiny part of the Earth's history.

Your early ancestors lived in bands and groups, so they could help one another. You follow them as they searched for shelter and food. They were mainly hunters and gatherers.

Sometimes, you stop at temporary camps, rock shelters or caves. You rely on hunting and gathering edible plants and fruits to survive. You use fire and make tools for easier lives.

You watch them make stone axes, blades, arrowheads and other tools. They communicate through languages that are now lost. You also learn about their beliefs about nature and possible ideas about life after death.

You can read life in rock paintings found in hundreds of caves. You make ornaments, such as beads and pendants, and sometimes exchange them. These discoveries connect your small group to a much longer human story.

You watch people settle down. They grow cereals and grains. They domesticate animals such as cattle and goats. You see living conditions improving for people in many parts of the world.

You walk towards a river, where many communities often settle. The land is worked collectively. There is no sense of individual ownership.

As more food becomes available, you see communities grow in size and number. You watch people exchange goods in villages. You see food, clothing and tools passing between them.

Finally, you see a chieftain caring for the community's well-being. New technologies include pottery and the use of metals such as copper and iron.

activities.title: Names Across Time
activities.body:
Begin your journey with modern India. It has defined borders and states. Its population is also known.

Now imagine looking back 500, 2,000 or even 5,000 years. You would find a very different India. Across this journey, you will meet many names for the Indian Subcontinent. Its boundaries have also changed.

Next, you visit the evidence used to trace these names. Old texts, travellers’ accounts and pilgrims’ accounts all offer clues. Inscriptions offer more clues too.

Your tour then reaches the Ṛig Veda, India’s oldest text. It is several thousand years old. Here, you discover that the Ṛig Veda calls the north-western region Sapta Sindhava. This means the land of the seven rivers. The name Sindhava comes from Sindhu. This word can mean the Indus River or a river in general.

Finally, you return to the modern map. You find defined borders, defined states and a known population. Remember how the Subcontinent’s names and boundaries have changed.

activities.title: A Tour of Regional Names
activities.body:
Imagine opening an old Indian book and beginning a journey through its regional names. The Mahābhārata is one of India’s most famous texts. As time went on, names for different parts of India appeared in old writings. You can travel through these names as a special tour.

You meet Kāshmīra, one of the many regions listed in the Mahābhārata. This name refers roughly to today’s Kashmir. Kurukṣhetra appears, referring to parts of today’s Haryana. Here, you begin to see how old names connect with places you know.

Moving onward, you find Vanga, which refers to parts of Bengal. You also meet Prāgjyotiṣha, roughly referring to today’s Assam. Kaccha greets you as another name for today’s Kutch. Each stop helps you recognise an older way of naming places.

Your tour brings you to Kerala in the Mahābhārata. The name was used there for roughly today’s Kerala. You wonder why these names matter to a social science lesson. They show how regional names were recorded in a famous text. Scholars think the Mahābhārata was written from a few centuries BCE onward.

activities.title: Two Names for One Land
activities.body:
Imagine you are reading the Mahābhārata. You meet two names for one vast land.

First comes Bhāratavarṣa. The text clearly uses it for the entire Indian Subcontinent. Under this wider name, you find many rivers and peoples. The name means “the country of the Bharatas”.

Then you meet Jambudvīpa. It means “the island of the fruit of the jamun tree”. The jamun is a common tree native to India. Later, Jambudvīpa came to mean the Indian Subcontinent.

Your tour reaches an older name: Bharata. This name first appears in the Ṛig Veda. Here, Bharata refers to one of the main Vedic groups of people. You discover how a name can grow from a people to a whole land.

As you continue, you hear of several kings named Bharata. Your final thought is simple: two names can describe one whole land.

It means “the country of the Bharatas”. Jambudvīpa means “the island of the fruit of the jamun tree”. The jamun is a common tree native to India. Later, Jambudvīpa came to mean the Indian Subcontinent.

activities.title: A Tour of Ancient India
activities.body:
You begin a journey through ancient India with Aśhoka. He lived around 250 BCE. The India under him included Bangladesh and Pakistan, and parts of Afghanistan.

Along the way, you find many inscriptions left by Aśhoka. These written marks help you imagine his presence. Then, a few centuries later, Bhārata becomes the general name for the Indian Subcontinent.

You open the Viṣhṇu Purāṇa, an ancient text describing Bhārata. The text describes Bhārata as the country north of the ocean. It also describes Bhārata as the country south of the snowy mountains.

Today, you still meet the name Bhārata. In northern India, the name is generally written as Bharat. In southern India, the name is often written as Bharatam. Different spellings now point back to the same name.

In another corner of your journey, you hear about an ancient Tamil poem. It came from about 2,000 years ago. It praised a king. Your tour now links Aśhoka's inscriptions with Bhārata's many meanings.

Today, people write the name Bharat in northern India. In southern India, they write it Bharatam.

lessons.title: How Persians and Greeks Named India

activities.title: How India Got Its Name
activities.body:
You begin your journey in Iran, where the ancient Persians lived. The Persians were the first foreign people to mention India.

During your visit, you hear about a military campaign. In the sixth century BCE, a Persian emperor launched it. The Persians gained control of the Indus River region. This area had earlier been called Sindhu.

As you look through Persian records and inscriptions, you find names for this region. They called India Hind, Hidu or Hindu. These Persian names were adaptations of the word Sindhu.

You learn that the ancient Persian word Hindu was only a geographical name. You also learn that it did not refer to the Hindu religion.

Next, you meet the ancient Greeks, who called the region Indoi or Indike. The Greeks dropped the letter h from Hindu. They dropped h because that letter was not in their language.

These names were changed forms of Sindhu. In ancient Persian, Hindu was only a name for the place. It did not refer to the Hindu religion. Greeks called the region Indoi or Indike. Greeks dropped h, which their language did not contain.

activities.title: Names on the Journey
activities.body:
Imagine setting out from ancient China, curious to learn what lay beyond its borders. Centuries ago, Chinese people and India knew of one another. Would this journey change what people called a place?

In the 7th century CE, you could follow Xuanzang from China to India. He travelled through many parts of India and met scholars. He collected Buddhist texts and later carried them home. His journey took him away for 17 years. Then you return with him to China.

There, Xuanzang translated the Sanskrit manuscripts he had taken home. Several other Chinese scholars also visited India over the centuries. Now you meet Tianzhu, another Chinese name derived from Sindhu. Foreign visitors mostly took their names for India from the Sindhu or Indus River. You might also understand Tianzhu as heavenly master.

Your tour ends with Hindustān, a name first seen in a Persian inscription. That inscription appeared about 1,800 years ago. Most invaders later used Hindustān for the Indian Subcontinent. So, as you travel through names, you uncover old routes of contact.

Hindustān first appeared in a Persian inscription about 1,800 years ago. Later, most invaders used this name for the Subcontinent.

lessons.title: What Is a Civilisation?

activities.prompt: What helps people build a busy, well-run society together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of a Civilisation
activities.body:
You begin your journey by wondering what a civilisation is. You find that it means an advanced stage of human society. Such a society needs some form of government and administration. These help manage society and its many activities.

Next, you explore how cities grow. Urbanism includes town planning, the growth of cities and their management. Town planning often includes water management and a drainage system.

After this, you visit people practising many crafts. You see goods made from stone or metal. Then you watch a trade exchange. Trade includes exchanges within a city or region, and with distant places. It can reach other parts of the world too.

Your tour now turns towards culture. You find it expressed through art, architecture, literature, oral traditions or social customs. You might notice it in a building design, a written story, or a shared custom.

Finally, you see productive agriculture at work. It provides enough food for both villages and cities. Your journey shows how government, towns, crafts, trade, culture and food production work together.

activities.title: What Makes a Civilisation?
activities.body: A civilisation is an advanced stage of human society. It needs government and administration to manage society. Urbanism includes town planning, city growth and city management. Town planning often includes water management and drainage. People make crafts from stone or metal. Trade happens within a city or region, and with distant places. Culture appears in art, architecture, literature, oral traditions and social customs. Productive agriculture gives enough food for villages and cities.
keyPoints: Civilisation needs government and administration to manage society.
Urbanism covers town planning, city growth and city management.
Culture uses art, architecture, literature, oral traditions and social customs.
activities.explanation: These parts help a civilisation manage society, make goods, trade, share culture and feed its people.

activities.title: Along the Harappan Rivers
activities.body:
Imagine beginning your journey beside the Indus River, where ancient settlements rose near its water. You follow the river and its five main tributaries. Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, and many other sites spread along these waterways. Life gathered near the rivers, and the settlements grew into important cities.

Sindh greets you on the next part of your journey. Harappa was the first city of this civilisation to be excavated. The Harappan civilisation was one of the oldest civilisations in the world. The people who lived there were called Harappans. The civilisation is also known by several names. These include Harappan, Indus, and Indus-Sarasvatī Civilisation.

Now, you turn towards the Sarasvatī River. Many sites stood along its course. This river is now called Ghaggar in India and Helmand in Afghanistan. The Sarasvatī River is first mentioned in the Rigveda.

As your tour ends, you see a special pattern. Rivers helped shape where people settled and cities flourished. Many Harappan sites stood beside these rivers. Your journey shows how closely rivers and cities were linked.

Harappa, in Sindh, was the first city excavated (dug up). Important cities grew along rivers, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.

lessons.title: Town-Planning

activities.prompt: How were early towns organised, and how were their streets planned?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Towns of the Indus Valley
activities.body:
Imagine joining a tour of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. You first visit Harappa and then Mohenjo-daro. These were the first two Harappan cities discovered. These cities were also the first of the civilisation to be discovered.

Your guide explains that many more sites were later found in the Indus plains. At first, this civilisation was called the Indus Valley civilisation. Other major cities included Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Banawali.

Now, you walk through a city built to a precise plan. Many streets point towards the cardinal directions. Most cities had fortification walls. Each had two distinct parts, an upper town and a lower town.

In the upper town, the local elite probably lived. Common people lived in the lower town. You pass large buildings used for collective purposes. Most of these buildings were generally made of bricks.

As your tour ends, you look across the walls and straight streets. You remember the city's precise plan. You also notice the large brick buildings used by many people.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Harappan cities were planned
activities.body: Big Harappan cities were built with careful plans. Many streets faced the cardinal directions (north, south, east and west). Most cities had walls for defence and two separate parts. Rich, powerful people probably lived in the upper town. Common people lived in the lower town. Some big buildings were for the whole community. Most of these buildings were made of bricks.
keyPoints: Streets often faced the cardinal directions.
Most cities had walls and two separate parts.
Rich, powerful people probably lived in the upper town.

lessons.title: Water Management

activities.prompt: How did ancient people manage water and keep their homes clean?

activities.title: Following the Water
activities.body:
You meet Harappans who gave great importance to water management and cleanliness. Their homes often had separate bathing areas. These areas connected to larger drains beneath the streets. The drains generally ran below streets and carried away waste water. You follow this network as you explore.

As you walk through Mohenjo-daro, you see hundreds of brick wells. People drew water from these wells. These wells were built from bricks. You can imagine drawing water during your journey.

In other regions, you might see people taking water from ponds, streams or reservoirs. At Dholavira, you find at least six large reservoirs. Most of these reservoirs were linked by underground drains. This network supported water harvesting and distribution.

Your tour ends beside the drains. You now understand why water management mattered greatly to the Harappans.

activities.body: Harappans cared a lot about **water management**. This means caring for water and using it properly. They also cared about cleanliness. Many homes had their own bathing areas. These joined bigger drains under the streets. The drains carried waste water away. Mohenjo-daro had hundreds of wells made of bricks. In other places, people may have taken water from ponds, streams or **reservoirs** (large water tanks). Dholavira had at least six large reservoirs. Most were joined by underground drains.

Home bathing areas joined bigger drains.

activities.body:

The rivers made the soil around them richer.
You see fields of barley, wheat, millets and sometimes rice.
Pulses and many kinds of vegetables also grow here.

They wove this cotton into cloth and made farming tools, including the plough.
They domesticated animals for meat and caught fish in rivers and the sea.

You follow Harappan traders travelling by land, river and sea.
They exported ornaments, timber, daily-use objects, probably gold, cotton and perhaps foods.
Carnelian beads were among their most favoured ornaments.

You learn that Harappans mastered working copper and made bronze by adding tin.
At Lothal, a huge dockyard received and sent boats.

activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Harappan Journey
activities.body:
You begin among Harappan city ruins. Archaeologists have unearthed many objects made and used by the Harappans. Games and toys amused both adults and children. You imagine adults and children playing with their games and toys.

Then you ask why this civilisation began to fall apart despite its achievements. The cities were abandoned one by one. Many inhabitants adopted a rural lifestyle in the changed environment. Most Harappans scattered over hundreds or thousands of small rural settlements.

You find no trace of warfare or invasion. Harappans seem to have had no army or weapons of war. The available evidence suggests a relatively peaceful civilisation. It appears that the earlier government or administration no longer existed.

A climatic change caused reduced rainfall and a drier phase. Cities such as Kalibangan and Anauli were abandoned.

Yet much Harappan culture and technology survived. It passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation. Your journey ends with the survival of Harappan culture and technology.

activities.body: Archaeologists have found many objects made by Harappans. They made games and toys for adults and children. Later, the Indus-Sarasvatī civilisation began to break down. It had many good things. But it still broke down. The climate changed. It had less rain and became drier. People left the cities one by one. Many people lived a rural life, in villages and the countryside. The evidence shows it was mostly peaceful.
