activities.title: A Tour of India’s Cultural Roots
activities.body:
Imagine standing along India’s cultural path, wondering where its earliest roots began. You find that Indian culture is thousands of years old.

Some roots lead to the Indus civilisation. You also meet schools of thought, which are groups of thinkers sharing similar ideas.

Now enter the world of the Vedas. The four are the Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda and Atharva Veda.

You listen as rishis and rishikas sing thousands of hymns, written as poems and songs. These hymns were composed in the Sapta Sindhava region.

You hear the hymns recited aloud, rather than written down. You see the texts memorised and passed on with very few changes. The hymns addressed deities such as Indra, Agni and Varuṇa. Finally, your tour reaches the last Rig Veda mantras, which call for unity among people.

The four Vedas are the Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda and Atharva Veda. They have thousands of hymns. Hymns are poems and songs. People said them out loud. People learned the texts by heart. They passed them on with very few changes.

activities.title: A Tour of Vedic Society
activities.body:
You begin your journey through Vedic society by meeting the janas, or clans. These groups formed early Vedic society. The Rig Veda lists more than 30 of them. You can imagine them spread across different regions.

As you travel, you hear about the Bharatas, Purus, Kurus and Yadus. Each clan was linked to a region in the northwest of the Subcontinent.

Now you arrive at a puzzling part of the tour. Here, you find that little is known about how the janas governed their society. The Vedas mention a king or ruler, using the word rājā. You also hear of the sabha and samiti, names for collective gatherings.

Next, you walk through a busy world of work. Vedic texts mention many different professions. Farmers, weavers, potters, builders and carpenters all appear. Here, you also find healers and priests.

As your tour ends, you see clans, regions, gatherings and workers. Every stop reminds you how varied Vedic society was. Some details remain hidden, especially about how clans governed themselves. The Vedas give you clues, but not a complete picture.

That area was in the northwest of the Subcontinent. The Vedas mention a king or ruler called rājā. Sabha and samiti were gatherings of people. Vedic society also had farmers, weavers, potters, builders, carpenters, healers and priests.

activities.title: Journey Through Upanishad Ideas
activities.body:
You begin with the Upanishads, which built on Vedic ideas and introduced new ideas. Imagine walking through a garden of questions about life, rebirth and what you truly are. Here, you learn about rebirth and the idea of karma.

Now you meet brahman, the divine essence. You also meet ātman, or the Self. The ātman is the divine essence present in every being.

As you wander further, you see that everything in the world is connected. One prayer wishes that all creatures may be happy. You imagine its wish reaching every creature.

Next, you enter the world of schools of thought. Several schools of thought grew from the Vedas. These schools became foundations of Hinduism as it is understood today.

Finally, you discover yoga. Yoga developed methods for realising brahman in your consciousness. Through these methods, you practise bringing your awareness within.

Ātman means the Self. Ātman is in every living being. The Upanishads teach that everything is connected. One prayer asks for happiness for all creatures. Some schools grew from the Vedas. They became the base of Hinduism. Yoga developed ways to truly know brahman in the mind.

activities.prompt: How can we understand why people suffer?

activities.title: The Buddha’s Journey
activities.body:
You begin your journey in India. There, a school of thought does not accept Vedic authority. You meet Siddhārtha Gautama, born as a prince in Lumbini. Soon, you face questions about human suffering.

At twenty-nine, you see an old person, a sick person and a dead body. These sights make you leave palace life. You search for the cause of human suffering.

You follow his path beneath a pipal tree, where he attains enlightenment. He teaches that ignorance and attachment cause suffering. People need sincere inner discipline. He also teaches ahimsa, meaning non-hurting or non-injuring.

After enlightenment, you see him found the Sangha. This community includes monks and later nuns. Buddhism has enormous influence across India and Asia. You also learn about the Buddha’s former births through the Jataka tales.

activities.title: Gautama's Search
activities.body: Buddhism is a school of thought. It is a set of shared ideas. It did not accept Vedic authority. Siddhārtha Gautama was born a prince in Lumbini. At 29, he saw an old person, a sick person and a dead body. He left the palace. He searched for the cause of human suffering. He sat under a pipal tree and meditated. He gained enlightenment. Enlightenment means deep understanding. He taught that ignorance and attachment cause suffering.

Ignorance and attachment cause suffering.
Ahimsa means not hurting or injuring.
activities.explanation: These ideas came from Gautama's search for the cause of suffering.

activities.prompt: Ready to explore how different schools of thought see life?

activities.title: A Tour of Jainism and Other Schools
activities.body:
First, you hear that Jainism is said to have roots much older than Buddhism. Then you meet Prince Vardhamāna, born into a royal family. At thirty, he left home to seek spiritual knowledge. After twelve years, he achieved supreme wisdom. He became known as Mahāvīra, meaning “great hero”.

Your next stop reveals what “Jain” means. The word Jain comes from jina, meaning conqueror. This conquest means overcoming ignorance and attachments. You now follow his search for spiritual knowledge.

Back with Mahāvīra, you explore his teachings. They include ahimsa, anekāntavāda and aparigraha. Anekāntavāda teaches that truth has many aspects. Aparigraha means non-possession and limiting material belongings.

You then consider Jainism’s view of living things. It stresses the interconnectedness of all living creatures. In your mind, each living creature connects with others. You look beyond any one creature.

Finally, you visit the Chārvāka school. They believed that only the material world exists. You also learn that the Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools shared important concepts.

activities.title: Roots of Tradition
activities.body:
Imagine you walk through a community, following teachings passed by word of mouth. You hear teachings and practices shared without written texts. These form an oral tradition, where learning moves from person to person.

Next, you see how common people carry folk traditions. They pass these traditions on to one another. No written book is needed for this sharing.

Now you enter a tribal community. A tribe is a group of families or clans. They share a tradition of common descent. People often share culture and language and live close together. Some may live under a chief and hold no private property.

You look back at ancient India. There was no separate word for tribe there. Earlier biased judgements about tribal communities have mostly been abandoned. You also learn that, in 2011, India had 705 tribes with about 104 million people.

Finally, you notice threads joining folk, tribal and Hindu belief systems. Many concepts are similar across them. Deities, concepts, legends and rituals have moved between traditions. This long interaction has brought mutual enrichment. You leave remembering that mutual enrichment grows from long interaction.

Folk, tribal and Hindu beliefs also share and exchange ideas.

activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: India’s Rich Diversity
activities.body:
Imagine boarding a train for a journey across India. You watch the land change. You see many kinds of dress and food. You hear languages that may sound familiar or unfamiliar. You also spot different scripts as your journey continues.

You may even meet people from other parts within your own region. People from different places may have different customs and traditions. You may notice their clothing, food and languages during your travels.

This variety of landscapes, cultures and ways of life is called India’s rich diversity. India has over 1.4 billion people, making such diversity unsurprising.

Have you heard of the Anthropological Survey of India? It is a national organisation. The survey covered 4,635 communities across all States of the country. It counted 325 languages written using 25 scripts.

Here, a migrant is someone living away from their birthplace or original community. India is presented as an example of unity in diversity.

activities.body: India’s rich diversity means its many landscapes, cultures and ways of life. A train journey shows changing landscapes, different dress and varied food. Languages you know or do not know may be heard. Scripts are different ways of writing languages. Customs and traditions are ways people live. People from other regions may live near you. India is an example of unity in diversity.

activities.prompt: How can shared ingredients create so many different dishes?

activities.title: A Tour of Indian Food
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a food tour across India. You will taste foods from different regions. Your journey starts with grains, the basic food for most Indians. You are ready to learn.

You explore a shared food landscape. You will find thousands, or even lakhs, of dishes and preparations. Some food grains are common throughout almost the whole country. Rice, barley and wheat are among the common cereals.

You also find pearl millet, sorghum and finger millet among the millets. Dals are among the pulses eaten in India.

Next, you meet familiar spices on your journey. Turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger are common spices used across India.

Here is the special secret of Indian food. Different combinations of shared ingredients create an endless variety of dishes. You return home with a new wonder. You now know how shared ingredients create endless variety. Your curiosity has led you to a delicious discovery.

activities.title: A Tour of Indian Textiles
activities.body:
You begin your journey among Indian clothing. You see styles from many regions and communities. Each has developed its own style.

Traditional clothes differ in material, yet they share some features. A sari is a plain, unstitched length of cloth worn as clothing.

Saris may be made from cotton, silk or synthetic fabrics. Famous silk types include Banarasi, Kanjivaram, Paithani, Patan Patola, Muga and Mysore. You find hundreds of varieties, each with its own colours. Some designs are woven into the cloth, while others are printed afterwards.

Now, travel back to when Indian textiles were exported as far away as Europe. Chintz, a type of printed cotton, became very popular there.

England and France later banned imports of Indian chintz. They wanted to protect their own products. Your tour ends beside these traditions, each distinct, yet sharing some features.

Chintz became popular there. England and France later banned Indian chintz imports.

activities.title: A Festival Tour of India
activities.body:
Imagine a festival tour of India. You will find an immense variety of festivals. You follow a map and imagine visiting celebrations across the country.

First, you visit places where a few festivals are celebrated across India. These common festivals are often celebrated at about the same time.

Your guide shows you a map. It displays similar festivals with different names across India around the same date. You begin to see the pattern.

During your journey, you learn about Makara Sankrānti. This festival marks the beginning of the harvest season in many parts of India. It is celebrated in many parts of India on or around January 14.

You continue exploring and see that many major festivals take place during October and November. The map helps you spot similar celebrations around the same date. You discover that similar festivals can have different names in different regions.

activities.title: Stories That Spread
activities.body:
Imagine opening two enormous storybooks. The Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata might fill about 7,000 pages together.

In one, the Pāṇḍavas fight their cousins, the Kauravas, with Kṛiṣhṇa’s help. In the other, Rāma receives help from his brother Lakṣhmaṇa and from Hanuman.

Within these epics, shorter stories focus on values. They often ask what is right and what is wrong. These questions invite you to think about right and wrong.

Now visit the Pañchatantra, a collection of stories with animals as the main characters. These stories have been adapted into almost every Indian language. About 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages.

Next, listen to folk versions of the two great epics. Many communities have their own versions of the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata. This variety shows how Indian culture values diversity while keeping sight of the unity that supports it.

Folk versions show that Indian culture values diversity and unity.

activities.title: A Tour of Family Life
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a tour of the many homes where people live. Almost everyone lives in a family, so family shapes surround you each day. The family is the oldest and most basic unit of society. As you explore, you will meet different family types.

First, stop at a joint family home. Several generations live together, and you see them moving through the same home.

Next, visit a nuclear family. It mainly includes a couple and their children. Sometimes, it includes one parent and children instead. These arrangements show you that family life can take different shapes.

Now, listen closely to family words in Indian languages. They often include more words for relationships than English. Curiously, most have no special word for cousin. Cousins are treated as brothers and sisters because all the children are closely connected.

As your tour ends, look at the children around you. Family ties create deep bonds among them. You now see different family types and relationships. You can recognise these bonds wherever you meet them.

Family ties create strong bonds between all the children.

activities.title: A Family Life Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting a family and watching its everyday life. Family relationships rest on love, care, cooperation and interdependence. Cooperation means working together. You see family members caring for one another.

You see parents raising children to become happy and responsible members of society. Children take on more responsibilities in the home as they grow up. Daily practice helps them take part in household life.

You watch children learn traditions and practices that their families follow. Doing one's duty is an important principle of Indian culture. The family teaches values such as ahimsa, dāna, sevā and tyāga.

Family members often give up their own needs to care for the family. Now you meet Shalini, whose family showed support by sharing what they had. Shalini was happy when everyone could get new clothes.

Before you leave, you remember that duties connect family life. You see cooperation, responsibility and support shaping family life. Families depend on love, care, cooperation and interdependence.

Doing your duty is important in Indian culture. Family members may give up things they need. Shalini's family shared what they had.

activities.title: A Tour of Community Life
activities.body:
Imagine walking through a village with your family. You meet other families and people nearby, all connected in different ways. Your family is connected with other families and the people around you. Such a group of connected people may be called a community.

You come together for different reasons. Some village people work together to support one another. You may also work together on land preparation, sowing and harvesting.

Your village community may share natural resources. These can include water, grazing lands and forest produce. Many community practices were rarely written down, but they are called rules. These rules give communities secure access to resources.

You see how communities organise festivals, feasts, weddings and other events. You also see members coming together for different reasons.

For smooth working, each member must perform their duties. Without this, a community cannot function smoothly. You can see people connect, organise events, share resources and follow rules. This is how a community works together.

activities.prompt: How can a community work well when people disagree?

activities.title: Keeping Communities Together
activities.body:
You arrive in a community where people have lived together for a very long time. Daily life brings questions about how everyone should act. Sometimes people disagree, and disorder can begin. Without shared rules, society could not function.

You first notice family life. Families usually expect children to follow simple rules at home. At school, rules apply to both students and teachers. During examinations, students must follow certain rules too.

You then step outside and join other road users. Road users must obey traffic rules. Some rules are especially important and are called laws. A government makes rules and makes sure they are followed. Governance means making decisions, organising society and ensuring rules are followed.

You may wonder whether these rules stay unchanged forever. They do not, because rules and laws can be changed. Citizens can also have a say about laws and rules governing society. By understanding rules, governance and government, you can see how communities work together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How rules help us live together
activities.body: People have lived in communities for a very long time. Living together can cause arguments and disorder. Society could not work if nobody followed rules. Families, schools, exams and roads all have rules. Governance means making decisions and organising society. It also makes sure rules are followed. A government makes rules. It makes sure people follow them. Laws are very important rules. Rules and laws can change. Citizens, the people of a country, can have a say about them.
keyPoints: Communities need rules to work.
Governance organises society. It makes sure rules are followed.
Citizens can have a say about laws and rules.
activities.explanation: Rules help people live together. Governance helps rules work.

lessons.title: The Three Organs of Government

activities.prompt: How can government help stop digital crime?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Tour of Three Branches
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting a classroom about digital crime. You hear that criminals can now steal money through digital methods. Digital technology has opened new ways for criminals to steal money. Learning about this case will show you how all three branches of government work together.

You first enter the legislature. An assembly of representatives of the people makes and updates laws. Lawmakers make new laws to fight cybercrime. They can also update or remove existing laws.

Next, you visit the executive. It implements or executes laws. This branch puts the new laws into action, helping the country fight digital crime.

Then, you arrive at the judiciary. Courts decide whether someone has broken the law. They can decide what action a person should face for breaking the law. Cybercriminals can be fined and sent to jail.

Before the tour ends, the courts check their work. They check whether a law is fair. They also check whether an executive decision is right. You now see how the three branches work together.

activities.title: How the Three Branches Work Together
activities.body: Digital tools give criminals new ways to steal money. Cybercrime means crime done with digital tools. Governments have made new laws to fight cybercrime. The legislature is a group of representatives (people who speak for others). It makes and updates laws. The executive puts these laws into action. The judiciary uses courts to decide if someone broke a law. These three branches of government work together.

lessons.title: Separation of Powers and Three Tiers

activities.prompt: How can three government parts stay separate and still cooperate?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Government
activities.body:
Imagine you visit a government building and meet three separate organs. Good governance begins when they remain separate. Each organ has an expected role, and none should act beyond it. You watch each one stay within its role.

Yet the organs still interact and work together. Each organ can check what another organ is doing. You see them act like careful teammates, without taking one another's roles.

You notice how checking helps create balance. When the organs are not working together properly, they can restore balance. Working together and checking one another helps them do this.

Now you travel across India's levels of democratic government. A democratic government works at several levels. In India, it functions at three levels. You see local, state or regional, and national tiers.

Each level deals with different matters. A problem at home is usually checked at home before going to higher authorities. You now see why good governance needs separation, cooperation, and careful checks.

activities.title: Working Together, Staying Separate
activities.body: Good government needs the three organs of government to stay separate. The organs are the three main parts of government. Each organ should do its own job. But the organs also work together. They check each other. They can bring back balance when things go wrong. India's government works at three levels: local, state or regional, and national. Each level handles different things.
keyPoints: Each organ should do its own job.
The organs work together and check each other.
India has three levels: local, state or regional, and national.
activities.explanation: Staying separate and working together both help good government.

activities.title: A Tour of India’s Governments
activities.body:
Imagine you are touring India and learning about its governments. You see local, State and Central levels. Each level has a different role during a flood, and you can follow their help.

You first visit a local government, which exists in India. Local authorities may deal with a small flood. When a flood affects several towns and villages, you look to the State Government. It can send rescue teams to help.

For a massive flood affecting vast areas, you look to Central Government help. This help can include relief supplies and the army.

Now you meet the Central Government. The President of India is the nominal head of the Central executive. The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central Government. You also see the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha working together. They formulate national laws.

Next, you visit a State Government. Its assembly is called the Vidhan Sabha. The Governor is the nominal head of the State Government. The Chief Minister is its executive head. You finish your tour knowing that different levels can help during floods.

activities.body: India has local, State, and Central governments. Local authorities can deal with small floods. The State Government can send rescue teams. The Central Government can help with huge floods. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha make national laws. The President is the nominal head of the Central executive. Nominal means head in name only. The Prime Minister is the executive head of the Central Government. The Governor is the nominal head of a State Government. The Chief Minister is the executive head of a State Government.
keyPoints: Local authorities can deal with a small flood.
The State Government can send rescue teams.
The Central Government can help in a huge flood.

activities.prompt: How can someone use knowledge and humility to serve a whole nation?

activities.title: A Leader for the People
activities.body:
You begin in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu, where Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam was born in 1931. You learn that his family was humble. The story introduces you to a scientist who later served the people.

He became a renowned scientist. You soon understand why he was called the Missile Man of India. You explore his important role in India's space and missile programmes.

Next, you see him serve as India's 11th President from 2002 to 2007. Even as President, he remained connected to the people. You recognise that national leadership did not separate him from those he served.

Your tour also shows why he cared about good education and innovation. Although his presidential position was nominal, he could make a positive difference. His example demonstrates the impact a leader can have.

His humility and dedication inspired many people. He encouraged young Indians to dream big and work hard. You finish by recognising his power to impact countless lives.

Innovation means new ideas. He encouraged young Indians to dream big and work hard.

activities.prompt: How can ordinary people influence decisions about the country they live in?

activities.title: Your Journey Through Democracy
activities.body:
Imagine your journey beginning with the word democracy. It comes from two Greek words. The word kratos means rule or power. Together, they mean the rule of the people. Democracy is a foundation stone of governance in most countries.

At State and national levels, you vote for elected representatives. MLAs represent people at State level, while MPs represent them nationally. These elected members discuss laws, problems and solutions in assemblies. India is a representative democracy.

Imagine yourself visiting an assembly. Elected members discuss laws and consider problems. They also search for solutions. In direct democracy, every participant's opinion is taken into account when a decision is made.

During elections in 2024, India had about 970 million voters. If you are an Indian citizen above 18, you can participate in elections. Your vote helps choose MLAs at State level and MPs nationally.

Now compare representative and direct democracy. In representative democracy, you elect members to represent you. In direct democracy, every participant's opinion is taken into account. Which route seems closer to democracy's literal meaning, rule by the people?

activities.body: Democracy is the base of how most countries are governed. The word democracy comes from two Greek words. Kratos means rule or power. Democracy means rule of the people. India is a representative democracy. At state level and national level, people vote for representatives. MLAs represent people at state level. MPs represent people at national level.

activities.prompt: How can a village council make everyday life better for its people?

activities.title: A Visit to a Village Council
activities.body:
You begin your lesson in a village in India. This lesson focuses on local government in rural areas. You notice how large and diverse our country is. India has about 600,000 villages, 8,000 towns and over 4,000 cities. Almost two-thirds of India's population lives in rural areas.

As you walk around, you meet a Panchayat, which is a village council. It brings government closer to the people. Local people can take an active part in making decisions. You watch them discuss what their area needs.

As you continue your visit, you learn that Panchayati Raj is a form of self-government. The system has three levels. Its work includes agriculture, housing, roads and water resources. You see how it helps solve local problems and promote development.

Before you leave, you see Panchayats helping local development happen. Their work stays close to local needs. You understand that local government works through people and their choices. Your tour shows a village council as a centre of self-government.

A Panchayat is a village council (a group that makes village decisions). Panchayati Raj means self-government. Local people run it. It brings government closer to villages. Local people can join decisions. They can solve local problems. They can help development (making life better) grow. The system has three levels. Its work includes agriculture (farming), housing, roads and water resources (water for people).

activities.prompt: How do villagers choose the people who guide their village?

activities.title: Meet Your Village Leaders
activities.body:
Imagine you live in a village and want decisions to begin very near your home. But what if you could help choose the people who manage village work?

Welcome to the Gram Panchayat, the level closest to rural people. Here, you learn that Gram Panchayat members are chosen directly by the Gram Sabha. The Gram Sabha consists of village adults who are enrolled as voters.

You watch as women and men in the Gram Sabha discuss matters concerning their area. After choosing the members, the Gram Panchayat elects a head called the Sarpanch or Pradhan. In recent years, more women have become Sarpanchs.

You also meet a Panchayat Secretary, who helps the Gram Panchayat with administrative work. The Secretary calls meetings and keeps records.

Many Gram Panchayats also receive help from an officer called the Patwari. The Patwari keeps records of villagers' land. Sometimes, the Patwari also keeps maps that are many generations old. During your visit, you see how village adults shape local leadership.

The Panchayat Secretary calls meetings and keeps records. A Patwari keeps land records and old maps for villagers.

activities.body:
You meet Dnyaneshwar Kamble in Tarangfal village. He became its Sarpanch through a tough election. He won against six other candidates. His motto was “lok seva, gram seva.” It means that serving the village is serving the public. You see how his guiding idea placed village service first.

Before you leave, you remember Popatrao Pawar. He received the Padma Shri award in 2020. The journey connects village service, women’s leadership, and environmental care.

activities.body:

Finally, you return to Panchayati Raj democracy. You see both direct participation and elected representatives. Together, these forms support villagers’ active part.

lessons.title: The History of Municipal Corporations

activities.prompt: How did cities begin caring for their own communities?

activities.title: A Tour of City Government
activities.body:
You begin your tour at Fort St. George. The East India Company issued a charter. The charter included the fort and nearby territories. It was issued one year before the corporation was established.

The corporation began on 29 September 1688. Today, you know it as the Greater Chennai Corporation. It is the oldest municipal institution in India. This journey shows how a charter could start a city corporation.

In 1792, an Act of Parliament gave the Madras Corporation power to collect municipal taxes. Proper municipal administration began when the city gained this power. You now see why tax power marked proper municipal administration.

Your tour continues to Bombay. The Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai was first called the Bombay Municipal Corporation. It was created in 1865. Together, these stories show how municipal corporations developed in India. You have travelled through the history of city government.

activities.title: From Charter to Corporation
activities.body: The Madras Corporation is now called the Greater Chennai Corporation. It was started on 29 September 1688. It is the oldest municipal body in India. activities.body:
Imagine you are walking through a busy city. Tall buildings rise around you, and crowds fill the streets. Many people rush past you, and the noise can feel louder than village life.

City residents may live independently and might not know their neighbours well. Yet you can still show community spirit when someone needs help. After heavy rains, a house collapsed. Think about how local decisions are made in your neighbourhood. Urban local bodies have elected representatives. These representatives speak for citizens and their interests. Members of village and urban local bodies are elected. In villages, community members also make decisions together.

In a village, people often know one another and help each other. They work together in the fields and celebrate festivals together. Back in the city, your voice remains just as important. activities.title: A Market Tour
activities.body:
Imagine that you are visiting a market. People exchange goods and services around you. A market is where these exchanges happen. You can exchange goods for other goods. Services can be exchanged for other services.

Watch the people working. Economic activities involve money or payment in money’s worth. Money’s worth is the monetary value a person places on an object. A fee is payment for professional advice or services. You pay this fee for such help.

Geeta Aunty receives a salary for serving the country. Her work is an economic activity because she is paid. Rohan receives a salary for working for a software company. His paid work is economic too.

However, not every activity brings payment. Activities are divided into economic and non-economic activities. Non-economic activities do not generate income or wealth. You see Rohan volunteering during the weekend. His weekend volunteering is a non-economic activity.

You also care for your grandparents. Youth doing this is non-economic. At the market, you saw money and exchanges. You also saw volunteering without income. Now you can tell the kinds apart.

Money's worth means the amount of money a person thinks an object is worth. A market is a place where people trade goods (things you buy) and services. Goods and services can also be swapped for other goods and services. A fee is money paid for expert advice or services. Non-economic activities do not earn money or wealth.

activities.prompt: How can you discover the value someone adds while making an object?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rajesh Adds Value
activities.body:
Imagine that you visit a nearby market and meet Rajesh, a carpenter. He buys wood there to make furniture. You see him pay ₹600 for the wood used in furniture. This payment shows an economic activity because money is involved. Such activities have value in terms of money.

Next, you watch Rajesh use special tools and other materials. His skill, time and effort help him turn the wood into furniture. This change creates a new form, so it is called value addition. Economic activities add value at every stage of a process.

When the chair is ready, Rajesh takes it to the market. He sells each chair there for ₹1,000. You compare this price with the ₹600 paid for wood. The remaining ₹400 represents the value added to the chair. This remaining value comes from Rajesh's skill, time and effort.

Buying the wood and selling the chair are economic activities because they involve payment. You can now explain Rajesh's work as value addition. You also learn that payment in kind means non-cash payment received for work.

activities.body: Rajesh is a carpenter. He buys wood for ₹600. He uses tools and other materials to build furniture. He sells each chair for ₹1,000. The extra ₹400 is value added. It comes from his skill, time and effort. Buying and selling are economic activities. They involve payment. Value addition means changing something into a new form. Payment in kind is payment for work, but not in cash.

You begin at home, where parents cook food for the family. You watch this care happen through their hands. Such cooking is a non-economic activity. It may not involve money.

Next, you help children with schoolwork. You see them receive guidance with their lessons. You also see grandparents cared for. These caring activities are non-economic activities.

Then you join family members helping to renovate the house. Everyone shares the work. This work is another non-economic activity.

Your tour now reaches a temple, a gurudwara, a mosque and a church. Here, sevā is seen. It contributes to society without expecting anything in return. A temple distributes prasād to its devotees.

At a gurudwara, a community kitchen serves food free to every visitor. You also find a langar at the Golden Temple. Finally, you remember why these activities matter. These activities may not involve money. Yet the value they create is important in our lives.

activities.title: Working Together for Cleanliness
activities.body:
You begin a walk through your neighbourhood with a broom. Today, you join the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, which works to keep our surroundings clean. It depends on the collective efforts of all Indian citizens. You are already showing this spirit.

At home, you keep your home and surroundings clean. On the street, you meet others cleaning streets and roads together. You also help clean parks and other public places. In community areas, people work side by side.

As you continue, you see how these efforts can make a clean home. They can also make your neighbourhood, society and nation clean. The lesson is simple: cleanliness grows when everyone contributes. You have seen why individual care and teamwork must go together.

Now you enter a festival where the community gathers. Van Mahotsav, celebrated as the festival of forests, brings everyone together. You join others in tree plantation drives. The festival creates awareness about the value of trees.

During festivals, people organise many activities. They decorate the place and share the food they cook. You leave ready to join your community's cleaning efforts.

It also teaches why trees matter.

lessons.title: The Primary Sector

activities.prompt: Which jobs begin with nature’s help?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Primary Activities
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting places where useful things begin. You soon notice that each place works closely with nature. These are known as primary activities, or primary sector economic activities.

First, you visit a farm. You watch grains and vegetables grow in the fields. Farmers do primary work because they grow food using natural resources. You also see poultry farms, where workers collect eggs. Getting eggs from poultry farms is also primary work.

Next, you travel to a forest. You see workers collecting wood from trees. Collecting wood from forests is a primary activity. The wood is a raw material taken directly from nature.

After this, you enter a mine and watch coal being extracted. Extracting coal from mines is a primary activity. Later, you visit fisheries, where workers take fish from the water. Taking fish from fisheries is a primary activity. Finally, you think about farming, fishing and forestry. These are examples of primary activities that depend directly on nature to produce goods.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is the primary sector?
activities.body: Primary activities depend directly on nature to make goods. This means people take raw materials straight from nature. These activities are also called the primary sector. Farming, fishing and forestry are examples. They include growing grains and vegetables, taking fish, collecting wood, and getting eggs.

They take raw materials straight from nature.

activities.explanation: The primary sector connects nature, raw materials and goods.

activities.title: A Tour of Secondary Work
activities.body:
You visit places where houses, roads and other structures are built. These activities belong to the secondary sector. You also provide water, electricity and gas. These are secondary activities too. Your tour shows many kinds of work.

Next, you enter factories and production units. Here, goods are manufactured and processed. You watch mills turn grains from farms into flour. The grains become flour.

Then, you follow wood from forests. You see it changed into furniture and paper. Wood from forests can become these products. This is another example of secondary work.

Later, you find cotton being used to make clothes. Workers turn cotton into clothing. You understand why factories and production units matter. They make and process goods. You know secondary activities build structures, provide services and transform materials into products.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Is the Secondary Sector?
activities.body: The secondary sector includes work that makes things and provides services. Builders construct houses, roads and other structures. Providers supply water, electricity and gas. Factories and production units manufacture and process goods. Mills turn farm grains into flour. Forest wood can become furniture and paper. Cotton is used to make clothes.

Factories and production units manufacture and process goods.
Raw materials become useful products such as flour, furniture, paper and clothes.
activities.explanation: The secondary sector makes goods and provides services.

activities.title: A Tour of Services
activities.body:
You begin a tour of the tertiary sector. You meet a fruit and vegetable vendor. The vendor sells farm produce to households.

Next, you meet a technician. The technician repairs and services electronic items, such as mobile phones and televisions. You also meet a mechanic, who repairs vehicles such as cars and tractors.

Further along, you meet an electrician. The electrician makes sure electricity is supplied regularly. You pause and learn about this important service.

After that, you try a mobile and internet service. These services belong to the tertiary sector. You then visit a hotel and a restaurant. Software development and services in these places are tertiary activities.

Before you finish, you put the tour together. The tertiary sector includes all these service activities. It is also called the service sector. You leave with a clearer picture of the work around you.

activities.body: The tertiary sector is also called the service sector. Technicians repair and service electronic items. These include mobile phones and televisions. Mechanics repair vehicles. These include cars and tractors. Electricians make sure electricity comes regularly. Mobile and internet services are part of this sector. Fruit and vegetable sellers sell farm crops to homes. Making software is a tertiary activity. So are services in hotels and restaurants.

lessons.title: The Story of the Anand Milk Cooperative

activities.title: The Anand Milk Cooperative
activities.body:
You meet Anand farmers. They milk their cows and sell milk to a nearby dairy.
Together, they approached Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel for advice.

As you follow their story, Patel advises them to form a cooperative.
This choice can make them independent and free them from relying on middlemen.
As a group, they take charge of collecting, processing and distributing milk.

You learn that AMUL was set up in 1946 CE.
You visit the factory that farmers set up in Anand.
You see the farmers sharing every task.
Sharing all the tasks helps them raise their income slowly.

During your tour, you see how milk production is a primary activity.
This is because milk comes directly from livestock.
You watch milk become powder, ghee, cheese and butter.
Turning milk into products is secondary work.

Finally, you follow AMUL products through transport, trade and retail.
These are tertiary activities.
You now see how shared work brought independence and slowly higher income.

activities.title: Farmers Build Together
activities.body: Farmers near Anand sold milk to a dairy nearby. The farmers went to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel together. Patel told them to form a cooperative. He also told them to be independent. A cooperative means farmers work together as a group. Independent means they do not need middlemen, or people in between. The group collected milk, processed it and sent it out. They built a factory in Anand. AMUL started in 1946 CE. Sharing work helped their income grow slowly.
keyPoints: A cooperative is farmers working together as a group.
AMUL started in 1946 CE.
Sharing work helped farmers raise their income slowly.

lessons.title: How the Three Sectors Work Together

activities.prompt: How does a book travel from raw materials to your hands?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Book’s Journey
activities.body:
Join a book-making tour and watch three sectors work together. You begin with natural raw materials, ready to become useful finished goods.

At each stage, you see why teamwork matters. Every step of making books depends on all three sectors working together.

During the tour, you look at how raw materials are turned into things people can use. Workers help carry out this work. Finished products are made for people to use or consume.

After you finish reading, think about the paper around you. Used paper can be recycled to make new paper. This gives materials another useful journey.

Recycling one tonne of paper saves 17 trees. It also saves space in places where waste is dumped. As you complete the tour, you see how recycling supports the whole process.

activities.body: The three sectors work together at every step of making books. They help turn raw materials from nature into finished goods. Used paper can be recycled to make new paper. Recycling one tonne of paper saves 17 trees. It also saves space where waste is dumped.
